paper.title: A Dynamic Theory of Nuclear Proliferation and Preventive War

edition.caveat: The user's private full-text index uses a different 50-page PDF layout; its PDF page numbers do not crosswalk automatically to this 32-page copy.
edition.page_numbering: One-based JSTOR PDF page number, and separately printed journal page.

verification.method: Visual inspection of actual typeset article PDF pages 5-12, particularly equation on PDF page 9 and game tree on PDF page 8
verification.appendix_note: The article explicitly places proofs of its propositions in a separate online appendix, which was not included in the uploaded 32-page article.

players.A: Monitoring/preventive-attack state; United States in motivating application

model.time: Infinite discrete periods, common discount factor delta in (0,1)
model.contested_stake: Unit interval; war winner receives stake in current and future periods, both pay costs
model.war: War immediately ends bargaining with costly lottery; A's pre-nuclear victory probability p, post-nuclear p_n<p; costs c_A,c_B>0
model.no_deal_definition: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium in which A does not offer B more than necessary to avoid immediate war
key_assumptions: B's investment is binary and its direct budgetary costs are abstracted away
Weapons development requires two stochastic prerequisites; the model begins in the early stage
B's nuclear acquisition becomes common knowledge, shifting A's victory probability from p to p_n<p
A receives noisy existence/investment signals and accurate or null stage/progress signals
A's offers can be accepted or rejected, and rejection causes immediate war
Source model's empirical application sets aside states expecting no gains from weapons

game_tree.first_period_note: Initial period begins without new intelligence signals; subsequent periods have signaling phase
order: Nature produces an imperfect signal about B's previous-period investment (tau or tau-prime, depending on previous action)
Nature produces an accurate stage signal with probability sigma, otherwise a null signal
A chooses immediate war or makes a take-it-or-leave-it bargaining offer x
B rejects (war) or accepts the offer
After accepting, B chooses whether to invest
Nature determines stochastic program progress and the game repeats if weapons not obtained

information.investment_signal: Correct positive signal conditional on investment with probability tau>1/2, and correct negative signal conditional on no investment with tau_prime>1/2; can be mistaken
information.stage_signal: True stage with probability sigma; null otherwise (baseline model)

proposition_1.scope: B is in the second stage, this fact is common knowledge, and the equilibrium is no-deal
proposition_1.investment: B always invests whenever given the opportunity

variables.p: A's probability of winning a war before B acquires nuclear weapons
variables.p_n: A's probability of winning a war after B acquires nuclear weapons; p_n<p
variables.lambda: Chance of stage-2 to nuclear acquisition in one round if B invests

proposition_2.scope: Second-stage-known no-deal equilibrium is immediate war
proposition_2.statement: In every no-deal equilibrium of the full game, B invests whenever given the opportunity.

proposition_3.scope: No-deal equilibrium with no new informative stage intelligence
proposition_3.statement: A's conditional probability that B reached the second stage increases with time without new stage intelligence.
proposition_3.if_epsilon_lt_lambda: Belief approaches (epsilon-epsilon*lambda)/(lambda-epsilon*lambda), which is less than 1

scope_notes: Do not treat page-level quote matching as proof of the associated interpretation.
The no-deal model's strategic assumptions need not hold in a bargain involving enforceable nonproliferation deals.
The proposition 1 inequality and figure 1 timing were source checked, not mathematically derived in this audit.
The source's appendix proofs and computational verification remain to be reviewed before any 'validated model' claim.
